client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and ever since then, family gatherings have just felt... wrong, I guess. Like there's this huge empty space where she used to be, and everyone else seems to be moving on, but I can't stop noticing she's not there. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: What you're describing — that hollow, unmistakable absence at gatherings — is such a real and painful part of grief, and it makes complete sense that it's still so present for you a month in. I also notice that even as you reached out today, there's a kind of quiet exhaustion underneath your words, like part of you isn't sure you deserve the space to feel this or that it will help. What would it mean for you if talking about her *did* make a difference?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if talking about her actually helped, it would mean I could go to family dinners without feeling like I have to hold myself together the whole time. But honestly, I'm not sure I even know what "making a difference" would look like — like, she's still going to be gone no matter what I say in here. It almost feels like letting myself feel better about it would be some kind of betrayal, like I'd be admitting I'm okay with her being gone, and I'm really not.
therapist: That fear — that feeling better somehow means accepting her loss or being okay with it — is one of the most common and quietly painful traps grief can set for us, and it's worth gently questioning whether healing really does mean that. Grieving her fully, and still missing her deeply, can actually be one of the most honest ways of honoring how much she mattered to you. I'm curious — what do you think *she* would have wanted for you at these family dinners?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: She definitely would have wanted me to enjoy myself — she was always the one making sure everyone had enough food and was laughing, she hated seeing people sad. But knowing that almost makes it worse, because I feel like I'm failing her by not being able to just... be okay. And part of me wonders if that's too easy of an answer, like maybe I'm just telling myself what sounds right rather than what's actually true.
therapist: The way you're questioning yourself — wondering if you're just saying what sounds right — actually shows a lot of self-awareness, and it's worth trusting that instinct a little. But I also notice you said all of that very quickly, like the words were tumbling out, which sometimes happens when we're circling something that feels both true and almost too tender to land on. What if the "easy answer" about what she'd want is actually just... correct, and the harder work is letting yourself believe you're allowed to receive it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That actually stopped me for a second, because I think you might be right, but believing I'm "allowed" to feel better feels almost impossible to just decide to do. It's not like I can flip a switch and suddenly feel like I have permission — it's more like there's this weight sitting on my chest that doesn't care what I logically know. I guess I'm skeptical that just recognizing it is enough to actually change how it feels at those dinners.
therapist: You're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't lift that weight — recognizing something intellectually and *feeling* it in your body are two very different things, and CBT isn't about flipping a switch. What we can do is work gradually on the small moments, like noticing when that weight eases even slightly at a gathering, and building from there rather than expecting permission to arrive all at once. What does that weight on your chest feel like it's actually protecting you from, if you had to guess?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think maybe it's protecting me from feeling like she's really, truly gone — like as long as I'm still carrying this grief so heavily, she's somehow still present in a way. If I let the weight ease up, I'm worried there's just going to be this emptiness underneath it, and that might actually be harder to sit with than the pain itself. It's strange to say out loud, but the grief almost feels like the last connection I have to her.
therapist: What you just said is one of the most profound things a grieving person can articulate — that the pain *is* the presence, and releasing it feels like a second loss. That's not strange at all; it's actually a very human way of staying close to someone you love. I want to sit with this with you for a moment — because what if the emptiness underneath isn't the absence of her, but actually the space where your memories, your love, and everything she gave you still live?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a really beautiful way to put it, and some part of me wants to hold onto that idea. But I'm also worried that it's the kind of thing that sounds meaningful in here and then just... dissolves the second I'm actually sitting at the dinner table with her empty chair. How do I make that reframe feel real in that moment, when everything around me is just reminding me she's gone?
therapist: That's exactly the right question to be asking, because the goal isn't to remember the reframe intellectually in that moment — it's to have something small and concrete to *do* when the empty chair hits you. In CBT we call these behavioral anchors, and it might look like something as simple as pausing to recall one specific thing she used to say or do at that table, letting yourself feel both the ache and the warmth of it at the same time. Would you be open to thinking together about what a small ritual like that might look like for you — something that brings her *into* the room rather than just marking her absence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I'm open to trying something like that, but I'm a little worried it might just make me cry in the middle of dinner and then everyone will be looking at me and I'll feel worse. She used to always say this specific thing when she put food on your plate — something in her language that basically meant "eat, eat, you need strength" — and even thinking about it right now makes my throat tighten. I guess I'm not sure I can hold both the warmth and the ache at the same time without one completely overtaking the other.
therapist: The fact that your throat tightened just now, saying her words — that's not a warning sign, that's actually her still living in you, and that's a beautiful and painful thing to carry. Your worry about crying at the table makes complete sense, but tears in front of family who loved her too might feel lonelier in your imagination than they actually would be in the room. What do you think would happen if someone *did* see you cry — is there a part of you that fears what that would mean about you, or how they'd respond?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think part of me is scared that if I cry, everyone will feel like they have to take care of me, and then I become this burden on top of everyone else's grief. There's also this other fear that's harder to admit — that some of my family members have already kind of moved on emotionally, and seeing me fall apart might make them uncomfortable or even a little impatient with me. I guess I've been telling myself I need to hold it together so I don't make things harder for everyone else.
therapist: You're carrying so much in that room before you've even sat down — managing your own grief *and* anticipating everyone else's reactions, making yourself smaller so others stay comfortable. I want to gently reflect something back: the belief that your grief is a burden is a thought, not a fact, and it's worth asking where you learned that your pain needed to be hidden to keep people around you okay. What would it mean about you, deep down, if you *did* let someone take care of you for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I think it would mean I'm weak, or that I can't handle things on my own — which is something I've always really prided myself on. I'm not even sure where that comes from, but it's deeply there, like if I need someone to take care of me it means I'm falling apart in a way that can't be undone. I guess I've never really questioned whether that belief is actually true or just something I absorbed somewhere along the way.
therapist: The fact that you're questioning that belief right now — asking whether it's true or just something you absorbed — is actually the first crack in a wall that's been costing you a lot. Needing support during one of the hardest things a person can go through isn't falling apart; it's being human, and the people who love you are likely not keeping score the way that voice in your head is. Where do you think you first learned that needing others meant something was irreparably wrong with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think it probably comes from watching my grandmother, actually, which feels strange to realize right now — she was someone who never complained, never asked for help, just kept giving and giving until there was nothing left to give. I think I always admired that about her, but maybe I also took it as a kind of instruction, like that's what it means to be strong and good. It's weird because the person I'm grieving might also be part of why I can't let myself grieve properly.
therapist: What you just uncovered is profound — that the person you're mourning also unknowingly handed you the very belief that's making it so hard to mourn her. That's not a contradiction; it's actually a sign of how deeply intertwined love and learned patterns can be, and it takes real courage to hold both her gift and the cost of it at the same time. I wonder if part of grieving her fully might eventually include gently releasing the instruction she never meant to burden you with — not as a betrayal, but as a way of loving her more honestly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
